---
title: Tables
description: How an item holds rows in a table its type declares, with typed columns, totals and changes you can undo.
---

Some things a person keeps are many small records under one heading: the bottles in a wine cellar, the lines of a budget, the messages of a conversation. Making each one an item would bury the item list. Instead, **one item holds them as the rows of a table**, and the item stays one thing to find, tag, link and move to the bin.

## Where a table comes from

**A type declares the tables its items hold**, each with named, typed columns. `core.conversation` declares a `messages` table, so every conversation holds its messages as rows, in the order they were sent.

**A `core.table` item chooses its own columns.** It's a table a person keeps by hand, such as a reading log or a list of contacts, and its `columns` property holds the column definitions. Other items of that type can hold quite different tables.

A column has a type, such as `string`, `integer`, `date`, `enum` or `item`, which holds the ID of another item. A column can be required, can say how it **adds up** (`sum`, `average`, `min`, `max` or `count`), and can be **searchable**, so search finds the rows that mention a word. [Define a type](/build/define-a-type#give-it-a-table) shows how a type declares one, and the contract's [tables](https://github.com/withmarfa/marfa/blob/main/conformance/spec/tables.md) chapter has the limits.

## A row is not an item

A row is its `id`, its `values` keyed by column, and when it last changed. **It has no version, tags, edges or history of its own.** It belongs to its item: a key that may read the item's type reads its rows, a key that may write the type writes them, and an item in the bin takes its rows with it.

Writing rows leaves the item's own `version` and `updated_at` alone. It moves the item's `last_activity_at` instead, so a list sorted by `last_activity_at` puts the conversation with the latest message first.

## Write rows in batches

Every write to a table is a **batch**: a list of operations on one table of one item, applied in order, all or none.

- **`put`** creates a row, or replaces the whole row its `id` names.
- **`patch`** sets the columns it names and leaves the others.
- **`delete`** removes a row.

This batch adds a bottle of Chablis to a cellar and corrects the count of another wine:

```http title="Request"
POST /items/01a1f141-38d8-7757-b9c1-b2e60b992c63/tables/table/rows
Authorization: Bearer <key>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "operations": [
    { "op": "put", "values": { "wine": "Chablis Premier Cru", "vintage": 2021, "bottles": 3 } },
    { "op": "patch", "id": "01a1f141-4d6a-7062-b447-f6ee16739f0e", "values": { "bottles": 2 } }
  ]
}
```

```json title="Response" status="200"
{
  "batch": "01a1f141-ad55-7133-88ce-e6fd8377da7f",
  "last_activity_at": "2026-11-19T00:42:55.701Z",
  "results": [
    { "id": "01a1f141-ad55-7133-88ce-e6fe9959a339", "outcome": "created" },
    { "id": "01a1f141-4d6a-7062-b447-f6ee16739f0e", "outcome": "patched" }
  ]
}
```

The item is a `core.table`, so its one table is named `table`. **When two writers change the same row, the later write wins**: a row has no version to compare. Send an `Idempotency-Key` with a batch you may retry, so a repeat is answered rather than written twice. From the CLI, `marfa rows write` sends a batch, and `marfa rows put`, `marfa rows patch` and `marfa rows delete` send one operation.

## Take a batch back

Each table keeps a **change log**: every batch that changed a row, with each row as it stood before. **Undoing a batch puts those rows back**, as a new batch of its own, so undoing the undo redoes it. An undo is refused with `undo_conflict` when a later batch has changed one of the same rows since; undo that one first.

The log keeps each batch for `row_log_retention_days`, 30 days by default. It's for taking back a recent mistake, not a history: `marfa rows batches` lists what it holds, and `marfa rows undo` takes one back.

## Read rows

A table's rows come a page at a time, in the order of the column the table names in `order`, or by row ID where it names none. **A read can filter and sort by any column** with the same filter grammar items use, written as `values.<column>`.

**Totals** answer how many rows a filter selects and what each column that adds up comes to, without reading the rows. For the cellar, that's how many bottles there are in all:

<Terminal>

```bash
marfa rows totals 01a1f141-38d8-7757-b9c1-b2e60b992c63 table
```

```text
row_count           3
totals.bottles.sum  11
```

</Terminal>

## Find and follow rows

**Search matches rows as well as items.** A hit for a row names its item and, beside it, the table, the row and the column the match came from.

**A link can point at one row**, written `[[Wine cellar#^<row id>]]` in a note's text. It stays a link to the item, with the row named.

**A batch that changes rows sends one `rows.changed` event**, with each row as the batch left it, so an app that follows the [event stream](/build/events) keeps its rows current without reading the table again. A device can hold a table in its [working copy](/build/devices) the same way, whole, and queue batches while offline.

Agents read and write rows through the MCP tools `marfa_read_rows` and `marfa_write_rows`. An [archive](/run/export-and-restore) carries every row.
